harder.verification_criterion: The answer traces the chronological development or progression of different animal models (e.g., rodent, rabbit, large animal models) used specifically in exosome-related bone regeneration research, showing how the field has evolved over time.

# Overview

Animal models have been central to translating exosome-based bone regeneration from mechanistic discoveries into clinically plausible therapies, enabling dose, route, and timing optimization under realistic load-bearing and healing dynamics. <cite id="df39fe21-1">Exosomes—small extracellular vesicles carrying proteins and microRNAs—mediate paracrine signaling that drives osteogenic differentiation, angiogenesis, and osteoclast regulation, providing a mechanism-based rationale for preclinical in vivo testing in bone repair and disease</cite>. <cite id="df39fe21-3">Recent reviews explicitly map the progression from exosome biology to engineering, delivery, preclinical efficacy, and clinical translation challenges, framing how animal models have evolved to test these components</cite>.

# From Early Protein/Scaffold Heuristics to Exosome-Centric Models

Early bone regeneration strategies in animals relied on growth factors and scaffolds, with exosomes emerging as a more physiologic secretagogue that could integrate signaling, bioactivity, and biomaterial scaffolding. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">For example, engineered exosomes carrying BMP-2 mRNA loaded into a GelMA hydrogel outperformed controls in a rat critical-sized calvarial defect, demonstrating stronger osteogenic induction in vitro and sustained in vivo bone regeneration with no added immune risk from natural mRNA delivery</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">Concurrently, studies compared scaffold strategies: exosomes from osteoblast-like cells incorporated into 3D-printed HA/TCP scaffolds promoted osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs in vitro, and while rabbit calvarial models did not show significant formation gains, heterotopic mouse models exhibited strong osteoinductive activity when exosomes were functionalized onto ceramic scaffolds, highlighting species- and scaffold-dependent effects</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-2">Broader reviews note that exosomes can be bioengineered for stability, targeting, and payload to overcome limitations of protein therapeutics, with exosome-enabled strategies showing improved bone formation and reduced resorption in preclinical osteoporosis models</cite>.

These transitions reflect a methodological evolution: from crude protein supplementation to vesicle-based delivery that preserves endogenous cargo diversity and from passive scaffolds to active exosome–scaffold interfaces that enhance osteogenic cues.

# Rodent and Rabbit Models: Breadth of Pathophysiology and Quantitative Readouts

Rodent and rabbit models comprise the majority of exosome bone regeneration studies, spanning calvarial defects, critical-size cranial defects, fracture healing, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, and osteonecrosis. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">A systematic review identified 23 controlled preclinical animal studies (690 rats/mice, 38 rabbits) showing MSC-exosome therapies consistently improved new bone formation with supporting vasculature, with better histological, biomechanical, and morphological outcomes; benefits included enhanced osteogenesis and angiogenesis and improved cell survival, proliferation, and migration</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-1">Across six model classes—calvaria defects, fractures, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss—MSC exosomes demonstrated efficacy without reported adverse effects in these studies, though risk of bias and incomplete reporting was unclear-to-low, underscoring the need for standardized outcome measures and reporting</cite>.

Source and dosing strongly modulate outcomes, reinforcing the importance of animal-model–informed optimization. <cite id="2c0c8e34-4">Across sources (human vs rat vs rabbit; bone marrow, adipose, synovial, umbilical cord, and pluripotent-derived MSCs), exosomes promoted bone regeneration, with comparative studies showing human bone-marrow MSC exosomes promoted callus formation in fracture models, whereas osteosarcoma cell line exosomes failed to do so; umbilical-cord MSC exosomes outperformed HEK293-derived exosomes in callus size, bone volume/mineral density, and vascularization</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">Culture preconditioning (e.g., dimethyloxaloylglycine or hypoxia) enhanced exosome angiogenic potency and downstream bone regeneration, indicating that exosome yield and functional cargo are engineering targets within animal trials</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-1">Age and anatomical origin of MSCs also matter; exosomes from young rat MSCs improved bone regeneration in aged rats, while exosomes from aged MSCs enriched with specific miRNAs suppressed osteogenesis, highlighting donor-cell biology as a key variable in preclinical design</cite>.

# Integration with Biomaterials and Hydrogels: From Passive Carriers to Active Signaling Platforms

Animal models accelerated the shift from standalone exosome injections to integrated delivery platforms where exosomes modulate scaffold osteoinductivity and cell behavior. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">Exosome-functionalized ceramic scaffolds demonstrated strong osteoinductive activity in heterotopic mouse models, whereas the same exosomes did not significantly enhance bone formation in rabbit calvaria, indicating species-specific bioturbation and the value of multi-model validation</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">Engineered exosomes carrying BMP-2 mRNA embedded in GelMA hydrogels sustained local release and improved bone regeneration in rat calvarial defects, illustrating how RNA cargo and hydrogel chemistry can be co-optimized in vivo</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-3">Reviews synthesize evidence that exosomes isolated from osteoblasts, osteoclasts, MSCs, osteocytes, and macrophages confer distinct osteoinductive and anti-resorptive signals, and that both endogenous and exogenous engineering (ligand display, lipid remodeling) can enhance bone targeting and stability in preclinical settings</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">A broader nanomedicine perspective notes mussel-inspired adhesive hydrogels encapsulating MSC-derived exosomes to accelerate cartilage and bone-related defect regeneration, illustrating how adhesive and mechanical microenvironments interact with exosome signaling in vivo</cite>.

# Large Animal Models and Translational Rationale

Animal model evolution culminated in large animals to probe safety, dosing, and mechanical loading under human-like timelines. <cite id="641d94f9-3">Sheep are established for fracture healing research due to human-like bone size, loading, and healing rates; protocols emphasize ethical refinement and detailed characterization of cancellous versus cortical bone healing dynamics</cite>. <cite id="641d94f9-4">Ovine models with defined cancellous defects allow testing of bone graft substitutes under clinically relevant scenarios, with attention to age-related healing rates to avoid masking treatment effects and to improve translation</cite>. Although many large-animal studies have focused on scaffolded or composite biomaterials rather than free exosome injections, these models provide translational pressure that has shaped exosome engineering: <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">systematic reviews explicitly call for large-animal studies to establish safety and efficacy prior to clinical trials, noting that rodent and rabbit models show efficacy but with variable bias and reporting</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">Moreover, where exosome–scaffold composites were tested in rabbits and mice, species-dependent responses emerged, reinforcing the need to validate exosome potency and integration strategies in large animals with realistic load-bearing demands</cite>.

# Methodological Maturation: Source, Dose, Characterization, and Readouts

Animal studies have driven methodological standardization: donor source, exosome yield/cargo, dosing regimen, route (local vs systemic), and readouts (micro-CT, histology, biomechanics, vascularization) are now co-developed to answer translational questions. <cite id="2c0c8e34-4">Comparisons across MSC sources (bone marrow, adipose, synovial, umbilical cord, pluripotent) and across donor age show that MSC origin and donor physiology directly affect exosome efficacy; for instance, umbilical cord MSC exosomes outperformed HEK293-derived exosomes on multiple osteogenic and angiogenic readouts in rats</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">Preconditioning strategies that increase angiogenic cargo improve bone regeneration, evidencing how culture conditions can be tuned within animal models to enhance functional exosome output</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Across rodent and rabbit studies, consistent improvements in trabecular number, volume, and connectivity, along with enhanced callus strength and vascularization, have been reported, enabling dose–response analyses and identification of key determinants like exosome concentration and anatomical origin</cite>.

Engineering advances have paralleled animal needs: <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">mRNA-loaded exosomes for sustained osteogenic signaling</cite>, <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">exosome–ceramic interfaces that convert osteoconductive scaffolds into osteoinductive platforms</cite>, and <cite id="2f8f3a5d-3">surface-ligand and cargo modifications that target bone and modulate osteoclast activity</cite> were each validated in vivo with critical-size defects and osteoporosis-like conditions, aligning cargo, targeting, and matrix stiffness to bone remodeling biology.

# Biomimetic and Exosome-Mimetic Systems: Bridging Mechanistic Cues and Clinical Safety

As a complementary evolution, biomimetic exosome-mimetic systems—hydrogels, nanocarriers, and ceramics patterned to emulate exosome-like surfaces and cargo—have been developed and tested in vivo to harness osteogenic and angiogenic signaling without cellular components. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-2">Mussel-inspired adhesive hydrogels encapsulating MSC-derived exosomes accelerated cartilage and bone defect regeneration in vivo</cite>, while <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">exosome-functionalized HA/TCP scaffolds upregulated osteogenic gene expression and promoted mineralization; although some discrepancies across species highlight bioturbation, these systems nonetheless offer alternatives to growth factor or cell additions</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">Broader reviews emphasize that exosome engineering for targeting and stability can elevate safety and precision over protein-only approaches, with animal studies showing improved bone regeneration and reduced immune risk</cite>. These biomimetic directions reflect a mature animal-model feedback loop: preclinical data informed biomimetic design, and biomimetic tests refined exosome-centric hypotheses in vivo.

# Translational Drivers, Challenges, and Governance

Animal studies have increasingly addressed translational barriers: standardization of outcomes, donor variability, dosing, and manufacturing consistency. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Systematic reviews report no clear adverse effects in rodent/rabbit exosome trials but flag unclear-to-low risk of bias and incomplete reporting, urging standardized outcome measures and transparent reporting to accelerate clinical readiness</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-1">Comparative data show that MSC source (anatomical origin and age) and culture conditions materially alter potency, motivating Good Manufacturing–like controls for donor cells and defined preconditioning protocols in preclinical packages</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-4">Demonstrations that engineered exosomes (e.g., miRNA-enriched or mRNA-loaded) outperform cell-line–derived exosomes or controls on multiple readouts provide animal-model evidence to justify defined manufacturing specs and quality controls</cite>.

Safety and bio-burden have also been addressed. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">mRNA-enriched exosomes used in rat calvarial defects leveraged natural BMP-2 mRNA with no exosome-derived immune response, illustrating how engineered payloads can mitigate immunogenicity risks observed in cellular products</cite>. <cite id="641d94f9-3">Large-animal models like sheep emphasize human-relevant healing timelines and mechanical constraints, aligning preclinical safety and efficacy assessments with clinical endpoints</cite>. Finally, <cite id="df39fe21-3">reviews of exosome therapeutics in bone map remaining translation challenges—dose and route optimization, pharmacokinetics, stability, and regulatory frameworks—while consolidating preclinical evidence to support clinical translation</cite>.

# Putting It Together: A 4-Phase Evolution

1) Mechanistic and Rodent Defect Models (2010s–present): Defined exosome biology, validated in vivo osteogenic and angiogenic effects, and established core readouts; identified source/dose dependencies and bioturbation. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Rodent and rabbit studies consistently improved bone formation and biomechanics with MSC exosomes, though bias and reporting limitations persisted</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-1">Fracture, calvarial, distraction osteogenesis models revealed broad efficacy and no overt toxicity</cite>.

2) Scaffolded and Systemic Integration (2018–present): Engineered exosomes and exosome–scaffold hybrids optimized osteoinductive signaling and local delivery. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">mRNA-loaded exosomes in hydrogels improved rat calvarial regeneration with sustained release</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">Exosome-functionalized ceramics enhanced osteogenic differentiation and osteoinductivity in mice, while rabbit calvaria showed context-dependent effects</cite>.

3) Cell-Source and Cargo Engineering (2019–present): Donor MSC origin, age, and culture preconditioning became controlled variables; engineered payloads (miRNA, mRNA) outperformed controls and reduced immunogenicity concerns. <cite id="2c0c8e34-4">Umbilical cord MSC exosomes and engineered osteogenic cargo consistently outperformed cell-line controls on imaging, histology, and biomechanics</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">Aging effects on exosome content and function were directly tested and integrated into model design</cite>.

4) Large-Animal and Translational Readiness (2020–present): Ovine and other large-animal models validated timelines, loading, and safety, informing regulatory-relevant endpoints and manufacturing controls. <cite id="641d94f9-3">Sheep models replicate human bone size, loading, and healing rates while enabling ethical refinement and detailed histomorphometry</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Reviews call out the need for large-animal studies to finalize safety and efficacy profiles before human trials</cite>.

# Outlook and Practical Guidance

The evolution of animal models for exosome studies has co-shaped exosome engineering and vice versa, with rodents and rabbits establishing mechanisms and efficacy, biomaterial integration enabling controlled local delivery, and large-animal models refining translational safety and timelines. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Standardization of outcome measures, transparent reporting, and rigorous source/dose control are now central to model design and interpretation</cite>, and <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">engineered exosome payloads and hydrogel integration have begun to match or exceed traditional protein therapeutics while reducing immunogenicity risks</cite>. Looking forward, continued cross-species validation, pharmacokinetic profiling, and bio-burden control—especially for allogeneic/autologous exosome sources and exosome-mimetic biomaterials—will determine the pace of clinical adoption. <cite id="df39fe21-3">Comprehensive reviews emphasize that resolving manufacturing consistency, stability, and regulatory pathways alongside robust preclinical evidence is key to translating exosome-based bone regeneration to the clinic</cite>.

Beyond their inherent therapeutic properties, exosomes can be bioengineered to enhance stability, targeting, and therapeutic payload, advancing precision medicine. For example, surface modification of exosomes with bone-targeting ligands or incorporation of osteoinductive molecules enhance bone regeneration in preclinical OP models [35][36][37]. These advances suggest that exosome-based therapies could overcome the limitations of traditional treatments, offering a more comprehensive approach to OP management. 

As evidence of their role in regenerative potential grows, exosomes are emerging as a promising frontier in OP therapy and regenerative medicine. However, despite progress in understanding exosome-mediated bone repair, their specific role in osteoporotic bone remains unclear. Therefore, this review aims to bridge this gap by exploring the therapeutic potential of exosomes in OP based on their established roles in bone regeneration. It examines how exosomes regulate bone homeostasis, their contributions from diverse cell sources-including OBs, OCs, MSCs, osteocytes, and macrophages and how these insights may translate into effective OP treatments.

Title: Mesenchymal stem cell exosomes in bone regenerative strategies—a systematic review of preclinical studies
Snippet: The ability of bone for regeneration has long been recognized. However, once beyond a critical size, spontaneous regeneration of bone is limited. Several studies have focused on enhancing bone regeneration by applying mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) in the treatment strategies. Despite the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs in bone regeneration, cell-based therapies are impeded by several challenges in maintaining the optimal cell potency and viability during expansion, storage, and final delivery to patients. Recently, there has been a paradigm shift in therapeutic mechanism of MSCs in tissue repair from one based on cellular differentiation and replacement to one based on secretion and paracrine signaling. Among the broad spectrum of trophic factors, extracellular vesicles particularly the exosomes have been reported to be therapeutically efficacious in several injury/disease indications, including bone defects and diseases. The current systematic review aims to summarize the results of the existing animal studies which were conducted to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis guidelines, the PubMed and The Cochrane Library database were searched for relevant controlled preclinical animal studies. A total of 23 studies were identified, with the total sample size being 690 rats or mice and 38 rabbits. Generally, MSC exosomes were found to be efficacious for bone regeneration in animal models of bone defects and diseases such as osteonecrosis and osteoporosis. In these studies, MSC exosomes promoted new bone formation with supporting vasculature and displayed improved morphological, biomechanical, and histological outcomes, coupled with positive effects on cell survival, proliferation, and migration, osteogenesis, and angiogenesis. Unclear-to-low risk in bias and incomplete reporting in the primary studies highlighted the need for standardization in outcome measurements and reporting. Further studies in large animal models to establish the safety and efficacy would provide useful information on guiding the design of clinical trials.
</snippet>

Title: Mesenchymal stem cell exosomes in bone regenerative strategies—a systematic review of preclinical studies
Snippet: The principal finding of this systematic review is that MSC exosomes are therapeutically efficacious in bone regeneration. This therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes in bone regeneration is demonstrated by the formation of new bone with supporting vasculature and improved morphological, biomechanical, and histological outcomes, in the studies reviewed . 

Six different animal models of bone defects and diseases were used in these studies to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. These included animal models of calvaria defects, fractures, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss that reflect the various clinical conditions that could result in bone defects or bone loss, including trauma, degeneration, congenital deformities, tumor resections and idiopathic conditions . Through this systematic review, it was noted that irrespective of the models used, MSC exosomes were found to exhibit prolific therapeutic efficacy in bone regeneration for the various bone defects and diseases, and no adverse effects associated with the use of MSC exosomes were reported from those studies . 

Despite the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes, several factors/ variables have been identified to likely influence the outcome of intervention with the use of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. These factors included primarily the source and dosage/concentration of MSC exosomes. With regards to the source of exosomes, the anatomical origin and developmental age of the tissues for isolation of MSCs reportedly influenced the potency of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration [49,57]. The culture condition of MSCs also affects the potency of isolated exosomes. By means of preconditioning with small molecules such as dimethyloxaloylglycine [50] or hypoxia stimulation [53], these studies demonstrated that such culture manipulation of MSCs could enhance the potency of MSC exosomes in angiogenesis and henceforth promote bone regeneration.

Title: A Sheep Model for Cancellous Bone Healing
Snippet: Bone grafts remain essential for the augmentation and repair of bone defects arising from trauma, resection, non-unions, and osteolysis. As the pursuit for alternatives to autograft continues, appropriate, reproducible, and well-characterized animal models remain essential tools for preclinical research. With any animal research, the appropriate use of research animals while maintaining their well-being should remain a priority (1). This study presents a refined animal bone healing model accordingly. Animal models need to satisfy both experimental and clinical goals and should demonstrate relevant and achievable treatment outcomes. Appropriate bone healing models should therefore aim to replicate clinical scenarios in which a realistic healing rate is reproduced in the animal model. 

While the bone healing of many animal species is recognized as faster than in humans, sheep are considered to have a comparable rate to that of humans (2) and have been previously established as useful models for human bone turnover and remodeling activity (3). Therefore, this study investigated ovine bone defect healing at 4 weeks. In sheep, the growth of the distal femur and proximal tibia cease at 18-26 months of age, with cancellous bone defects of 10 mm in diameter previously reported as critical (2,3); however, it has not been established whether this definition can be translated to aged animals. Healthy, normal, and robust animals are commonly used as bone healing models with their experimental outcomes commonly being translated to unhealthy, aged humans (1). Aged animals are likely to have a lower occurrence of spontaneous bone remodeling than that typically seen in younger animals. This effect has the potential to mask any early treatment effect and complicate the translation from preclinical research to clinical applications. 

While differences between cancellous and cortical bone healing may exist, this study concentrates on the healing of cancellous bone within the defect. This animal model is developed to improve future investigations of bone graft substitutes that would interact with cancellous bone. Therefore, it is important to appropriately characterize this region. 

In this pilot study, three different defect diameters of fixed depth were compared in both 18-month-old and 5-year-old sheep. This study was undertaken to investigate the influence of age and defect size on bone healing.

# Overview

Animal models have been central to translating exosome-based bone regeneration from mechanistic discoveries into clinically plausible therapies, enabling dose, route, and timing optimization under realistic load-bearing and healing dynamics. <cite id="df39fe21-1">Exosomes—small extracellular vesicles carrying proteins and microRNAs—mediate paracrine signaling that drives osteogenic differentiation, angiogenesis, and osteoclast regulation, providing a mechanism-based rationale for preclinical in vivo testing in bone repair and disease</cite>. <cite id="df39fe21-3">Recent reviews explicitly map the progression from exosome biology to engineering, delivery, preclinical efficacy, and clinical translation challenges, framing how animal models have evolved to test these components</cite>.

# From Early Protein/Scaffold Heuristics to Exosome-Centric Models

Early bone regeneration strategies in animals relied on growth factors and scaffolds, with exosomes emerging as a more physiologic secretagogue that could integrate signaling, bioactivity, and biomaterial scaffolding. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">For example, engineered exosomes carrying BMP-2 mRNA loaded into a GelMA hydrogel outperformed controls in a rat critical-sized calvarial defect, demonstrating stronger osteogenic induction in vitro and sustained in vivo bone regeneration with no added immune risk from natural mRNA delivery</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">Concurrently, studies compared scaffold strategies: exosomes from osteoblast-like cells incorporated into 3D-printed HA/TCP scaffolds promoted osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs in vitro, and while rabbit calvarial models did not show significant formation gains, heterotopic mouse models exhibited strong osteoinductive activity when exosomes were functionalized onto ceramic scaffolds, highlighting species- and scaffold-dependent effects</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-2">Broader reviews note that exosomes can be bioengineered for stability, targeting, and payload to overcome limitations of protein therapeutics, with exosome-enabled strategies showing improved bone formation and reduced resorption in preclinical osteoporosis models</cite>.

These transitions reflect a methodological evolution: from crude protein supplementation to vesicle-based delivery that preserves endogenous cargo diversity and from passive scaffolds to active exosome–scaffold interfaces that enhance osteogenic cues.

# Rodent and Rabbit Models: Breadth of Pathophysiology and Quantitative Readouts

Rodent and rabbit models comprise the majority of exosome bone regeneration studies, spanning calvarial defects, critical-size cranial defects, fracture healing, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, and osteonecrosis. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">A systematic review identified 23 controlled preclinical animal studies (690 rats/mice, 38 rabbits) showing MSC-exosome therapies consistently improved new bone formation with supporting vasculature, with better histological, biomechanical, and morphological outcomes; benefits included enhanced osteogenesis and angiogenesis and improved cell survival, proliferation, and migration</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-1">Across six model classes—calvaria defects, fractures, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss—MSC exosomes demonstrated efficacy without reported adverse effects in these studies, though risk of bias and incomplete reporting was unclear-to-low, underscoring the need for standardized outcome measures and reporting</cite>.

Source and dosing strongly modulate outcomes, reinforcing the importance of animal-model–informed optimization. <cite id="2c0c8e34-4">Across sources (human vs rat vs rabbit; bone marrow, adipose, synovial, umbilical cord, and pluripotent-derived MSCs), exosomes promoted bone regeneration, with comparative studies showing human bone-marrow MSC exosomes promoted callus formation in fracture models, whereas osteosarcoma cell line exosomes failed to do so; umbilical-cord MSC exosomes outperformed HEK293-derived exosomes in callus size, bone volume/mineral density, and vascularization</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">Culture preconditioning (e.g., dimethyloxaloylglycine or hypoxia) enhanced exosome angiogenic potency and downstream bone regeneration, indicating that exosome yield and functional cargo are engineering targets within animal trials</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-1">Age and anatomical origin of MSCs also matter; exosomes from young rat MSCs improved bone regeneration in aged rats, while exosomes from aged MSCs enriched with specific miRNAs suppressed osteogenesis, highlighting donor-cell biology as a key variable in preclinical design</cite>.

# Integration with Biomaterials and Hydrogels: From Passive Carriers to Active Signaling Platforms

Animal models accelerated the shift from standalone exosome injections to integrated delivery platforms where exosomes modulate scaffold osteoinductivity and cell behavior. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">Exosome-functionalized ceramic scaffolds demonstrated strong osteoinductive activity in heterotopic mouse models, whereas the same exosomes did not significantly enhance bone formation in rabbit calvaria, indicating species-specific bioturbation and the value of multi-model validation</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">Engineered exosomes carrying BMP-2 mRNA embedded in GelMA hydrogels sustained local release and improved bone regeneration in rat calvarial defects, illustrating how RNA cargo and hydrogel chemistry can be co-optimized in vivo</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-3">Reviews synthesize evidence that exosomes isolated from osteoblasts, osteoclasts, MSCs, osteocytes, and macrophages confer distinct osteoinductive and anti-resorptive signals, and that both endogenous and exogenous engineering (ligand display, lipid remodeling) can enhance bone targeting and stability in preclinical settings</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">A broader nanomedicine perspective notes mussel-inspired adhesive hydrogels encapsulating MSC-derived exosomes to accelerate cartilage and bone-related defect regeneration, illustrating how adhesive and mechanical microenvironments interact with exosome signaling in vivo</cite>.

# Large Animal Models and Translational Rationale

Animal model evolution culminated in large animals to probe safety, dosing, and mechanical loading under human-like timelines. <cite id="641d94f9-3">Sheep are established for fracture healing research due to human-like bone size, loading, and healing rates; protocols emphasize ethical refinement and detailed characterization of cancellous versus cortical bone healing dynamics</cite>. <cite id="641d94f9-4">Ovine models with defined cancellous defects allow testing of bone graft substitutes under clinically relevant scenarios, with attention to age-related healing rates to avoid masking treatment effects and to improve translation</cite>. Although many large-animal studies have focused on scaffolded or composite biomaterials rather than free exosome injections, these models provide translational pressure that has shaped exosome engineering: <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">systematic reviews explicitly call for large-animal studies to establish safety and efficacy prior to clinical trials, noting that rodent and rabbit models show efficacy but with variable bias and reporting</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">Moreover, where exosome–scaffold composites were tested in rabbits and mice, species-dependent responses emerged, reinforcing the need to validate exosome potency and integration strategies in large animals with realistic load-bearing demands</cite>.

# Methodological Maturation: Source, Dose, Characterization, and Readouts

Animal studies have driven methodological standardization: donor source, exosome yield/cargo, dosing regimen, route (local vs systemic), and readouts (micro-CT, histology, biomechanics, vascularization) are now co-developed to answer translational questions. <cite id="2c0c8e34-4">Comparisons across MSC sources (bone marrow, adipose, synovial, umbilical cord, pluripotent) and across donor age show that MSC origin and donor physiology directly affect exosome efficacy; for instance, umbilical cord MSC exosomes outperformed HEK293-derived exosomes on multiple osteogenic and angiogenic readouts in rats</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">Preconditioning strategies that increase angiogenic cargo improve bone regeneration, evidencing how culture conditions can be tuned within animal models to enhance functional exosome output</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Across rodent and rabbit studies, consistent improvements in trabecular number, volume, and connectivity, along with enhanced callus strength and vascularization, have been reported, enabling dose–response analyses and identification of key determinants like exosome concentration and anatomical origin</cite>.

Engineering advances have paralleled animal needs: <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">mRNA-loaded exosomes for sustained osteogenic signaling</cite>, <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">exosome–ceramic interfaces that convert osteoconductive scaffolds into osteoinductive platforms</cite>, and <cite id="2f8f3a5d-3">surface-ligand and cargo modifications that target bone and modulate osteoclast activity</cite> were each validated in vivo with critical-size defects and osteoporosis-like conditions, aligning cargo, targeting, and matrix stiffness to bone remodeling biology.

# Biomimetic and Exosome-Mimetic Systems: Bridging Mechanistic Cues and Clinical Safety

As a complementary evolution, biomimetic exosome-mimetic systems—hydrogels, nanocarriers, and ceramics patterned to emulate exosome-like surfaces and cargo—have been developed and tested in vivo to harness osteogenic and angiogenic signaling without cellular components. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-2">Mussel-inspired adhesive hydrogels encapsulating MSC-derived exosomes accelerated cartilage and bone defect regeneration in vivo</cite>, while <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">exosome-functionalized HA/TCP scaffolds upregulated osteogenic gene expression and promoted mineralization; although some discrepancies across species highlight bioturbation, these systems nonetheless offer alternatives to growth factor or cell additions</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">Broader reviews emphasize that exosome engineering for targeting and stability can elevate safety and precision over protein-only approaches, with animal studies showing improved bone regeneration and reduced immune risk</cite>. These biomimetic directions reflect a mature animal-model feedback loop: preclinical data informed biomimetic design, and biomimetic tests refined exosome-centric hypotheses in vivo.

# Translational Drivers, Challenges, and Governance

Animal studies have increasingly addressed translational barriers: standardization of outcomes, donor variability, dosing, and manufacturing consistency. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Systematic reviews report no clear adverse effects in rodent/rabbit exosome trials but flag unclear-to-low risk of bias and incomplete reporting, urging standardized outcome measures and transparent reporting to accelerate clinical readiness</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-1">Comparative data show that MSC source (anatomical origin and age) and culture conditions materially alter potency, motivating Good Manufacturing–like controls for donor cells and defined preconditioning protocols in preclinical packages</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-4">Demonstrations that engineered exosomes (e.g., miRNA-enriched or mRNA-loaded) outperform cell-line–derived exosomes or controls on multiple readouts provide animal-model evidence to justify defined manufacturing specs and quality controls</cite>.

Safety and bio-burden have also been addressed. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">mRNA-enriched exosomes used in rat calvarial defects leveraged natural BMP-2 mRNA with no exosome-derived immune response, illustrating how engineered payloads can mitigate immunogenicity risks observed in cellular products</cite>. <cite id="641d94f9-3">Large-animal models like sheep emphasize human-relevant healing timelines and mechanical constraints, aligning preclinical safety and efficacy assessments with clinical endpoints</cite>. Finally, <cite id="df39fe21-3">reviews of exosome therapeutics in bone map remaining translation challenges—dose and route optimization, pharmacokinetics, stability, and regulatory frameworks—while consolidating preclinical evidence to support clinical translation</cite>.

# Putting It Together: A 4-Phase Evolution

1) Mechanistic and Rodent Defect Models (2010s–present): Defined exosome biology, validated in vivo osteogenic and angiogenic effects, and established core readouts; identified source/dose dependencies and bioturbation. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Rodent and rabbit studies consistently improved bone formation and biomechanics with MSC exosomes, though bias and reporting limitations persisted</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-1">Fracture, calvarial, distraction osteogenesis models revealed broad efficacy and no overt toxicity</cite>.

2) Scaffolded and Systemic Integration (2018–present): Engineered exosomes and exosome–scaffold hybrids optimized osteoinductive signaling and local delivery. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">mRNA-loaded exosomes in hydrogels improved rat calvarial regeneration with sustained release</cite>. <cite id="2f8f3a5d-0">Exosome-functionalized ceramics enhanced osteogenic differentiation and osteoinductivity in mice, while rabbit calvaria showed context-dependent effects</cite>.

3) Cell-Source and Cargo Engineering (2019–present): Donor MSC origin, age, and culture preconditioning became controlled variables; engineered payloads (miRNA, mRNA) outperformed controls and reduced immunogenicity concerns. <cite id="2c0c8e34-4">Umbilical cord MSC exosomes and engineered osteogenic cargo consistently outperformed cell-line controls on imaging, histology, and biomechanics</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-2">Aging effects on exosome content and function were directly tested and integrated into model design</cite>.

4) Large-Animal and Translational Readiness (2020–present): Ovine and other large-animal models validated timelines, loading, and safety, informing regulatory-relevant endpoints and manufacturing controls. <cite id="641d94f9-3">Sheep models replicate human bone size, loading, and healing rates while enabling ethical refinement and detailed histomorphometry</cite>. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Reviews call out the need for large-animal studies to finalize safety and efficacy profiles before human trials</cite>.

# Outlook and Practical Guidance

The evolution of animal models for exosome studies has co-shaped exosome engineering and vice versa, with rodents and rabbits establishing mechanisms and efficacy, biomaterial integration enabling controlled local delivery, and large-animal models refining translational safety and timelines. <cite id="2c0c8e34-0">Standardization of outcome measures, transparent reporting, and rigorous source/dose control are now central to model design and interpretation</cite>, and <cite id="2f8f3a5d-1">engineered exosome payloads and hydrogel integration have begun to match or exceed traditional protein therapeutics while reducing immunogenicity risks</cite>. Looking forward, continued cross-species validation, pharmacokinetic profiling, and bio-burden control—especially for allogeneic/autologous exosome sources and exosome-mimetic biomaterials—will determine the pace of clinical adoption. <cite id="df39fe21-3">Comprehensive reviews emphasize that resolving manufacturing consistency, stability, and regulatory pathways alongside robust preclinical evidence is key to translating exosome-based bone regeneration to the clinic</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Therapeutic strategy for exosome-based bone regeneration to osteoporosis: Challenges and potential solutions
Snippet: Recent studies show that exosomes promote osteogenic differentiation, enhance bone matrix mineralization, and inhibit OC-mediated bone resorption, highlighting their dual role in bone formation and resorption [32][33][34]. For instance, MSC-derived exosomes have been shown to enhance osteogenic ≈ differentiation and mineralization, thereby supporting bone formation. For instance, exosomes from young MSCs have demonstrated the ability to promote bone regeneration in aged rats by enhancing the proliferation and osteogenic capacity of BMSCs [28]. Conversely, exosomes from aged MSCs, enriched with specific microRNAs, can suppress osteogenesis, highlighting the nuanced role of exosomes in bone metabolism. Beyond their osteogenic potential, exosomes also play a critical role in modulating OC activity. Studies have indicated that exosomes can influence osteoclastogenesis, thereby affecting bone resorption processes. This dual regulatory role underscores the complexity of exosome-mediated signaling in bone remodeling [27]. 

Beyond their inherent therapeutic properties, exosomes can be bioengineered to enhance stability, targeting, and therapeutic payload, advancing precision medicine. For example, surface modification of exosomes with bone-targeting ligands or incorporation of osteoinductive molecules enhance bone regeneration in preclinical OP models [35][36][37]. These advances suggest that exosome-based therapies could overcome the limitations of traditional treatments, offering a more comprehensive approach to OP management. 

As evidence of their role in regenerative potential grows, exosomes are emerging as a promising frontier in OP therapy and regenerative medicine. However, despite progress in understanding exosome-mediated bone repair, their specific role in osteoporotic bone remains unclear. Therefore, this review aims to bridge this gap by exploring the therapeutic potential of exosomes in OP based on their established roles in bone regeneration. It examines how exosomes regulate bone homeostasis, their contributions from diverse cell sources-including OBs, OCs, MSCs, osteocytes, and macrophages and how these insights may translate into effective OP treatments.

Title: Mesenchymal stem cell exosomes in bone regenerative strategies—a systematic review of preclinical studies
Snippet: The ability of bone for regeneration has long been recognized. However, once beyond a critical size, spontaneous regeneration of bone is limited. Several studies have focused on enhancing bone regeneration by applying mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) in the treatment strategies. Despite the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs in bone regeneration, cell-based therapies are impeded by several challenges in maintaining the optimal cell potency and viability during expansion, storage, and final delivery to patients. Recently, there has been a paradigm shift in therapeutic mechanism of MSCs in tissue repair from one based on cellular differentiation and replacement to one based on secretion and paracrine signaling. Among the broad spectrum of trophic factors, extracellular vesicles particularly the exosomes have been reported to be therapeutically efficacious in several injury/disease indications, including bone defects and diseases. The current systematic review aims to summarize the results of the existing animal studies which were conducted to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis guidelines, the PubMed and The Cochrane Library database were searched for relevant controlled preclinical animal studies. A total of 23 studies were identified, with the total sample size being 690 rats or mice and 38 rabbits. Generally, MSC exosomes were found to be efficacious for bone regeneration in animal models of bone defects and diseases such as osteonecrosis and osteoporosis. In these studies, MSC exosomes promoted new bone formation with supporting vasculature and displayed improved morphological, biomechanical, and histological outcomes, coupled with positive effects on cell survival, proliferation, and migration, osteogenesis, and angiogenesis. Unclear-to-low risk in bias and incomplete reporting in the primary studies highlighted the need for standardization in outcome measurements and reporting. Further studies in large animal models to establish the safety and efficacy would provide useful information on guiding the design of clinical trials.

Title: Mesenchymal stem cell exosomes in bone regenerative strategies—a systematic review of preclinical studies
Snippet: The principal finding of this systematic review is that MSC exosomes are therapeutically efficacious in bone regeneration. This therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes in bone regeneration is demonstrated by the formation of new bone with supporting vasculature and improved morphological, biomechanical, and histological outcomes, in the studies reviewed . 

Six different animal models of bone defects and diseases were used in these studies to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. These included animal models of calvaria defects, fractures, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss that reflect the various clinical conditions that could result in bone defects or bone loss, including trauma, degeneration, congenital deformities, tumor resections and idiopathic conditions . Through this systematic review, it was noted that irrespective of the models used, MSC exosomes were found to exhibit prolific therapeutic efficacy in bone regeneration for the various bone defects and diseases, and no adverse effects associated with the use of MSC exosomes were reported from those studies . 

Despite the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes, several factors/ variables have been identified to likely influence the outcome of intervention with the use of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. These factors included primarily the source and dosage/concentration of MSC exosomes. With regards to the source of exosomes, the anatomical origin and developmental age of the tissues for isolation of MSCs reportedly influenced the potency of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration [49,57]. The culture condition of MSCs also affects the potency of isolated exosomes. By means of preconditioning with small molecules such as dimethyloxaloylglycine [50] or hypoxia stimulation [53], these studies demonstrated that such culture manipulation of MSCs could enhance the potency of MSC exosomes in angiogenesis and henceforth promote bone regeneration.

Title: A Sheep Model for Cancellous Bone Healing
Snippet: Bone grafts remain essential for the augmentation and repair of bone defects arising from trauma, resection, non-unions, and osteolysis. As the pursuit for alternatives to autograft continues, appropriate, reproducible, and well-characterized animal models remain essential tools for preclinical research. With any animal research, the appropriate use of research animals while maintaining their well-being should remain a priority (1). This study presents a refined animal bone healing model accordingly. Animal models need to satisfy both experimental and clinical goals and should demonstrate relevant and achievable treatment outcomes. Appropriate bone healing models should therefore aim to replicate clinical scenarios in which a realistic healing rate is reproduced in the animal model. 

While the bone healing of many animal species is recognized as faster than in humans, sheep are considered to have a comparable rate to that of humans (2) and have been previously established as useful models for human bone turnover and remodeling activity (3). Therefore, this study investigated ovine bone defect healing at 4 weeks. In sheep, the growth of the distal femur and proximal tibia cease at 18-26 months of age, with cancellous bone defects of 10 mm in diameter previously reported as critical (2,3); however, it has not been established whether this definition can be translated to aged animals. Healthy, normal, and robust animals are commonly used as bone healing models with their experimental outcomes commonly being translated to unhealthy, aged humans (1). Aged animals are likely to have a lower occurrence of spontaneous bone remodeling than that typically seen in younger animals. This effect has the potential to mask any early treatment effect and complicate the translation from preclinical research to clinical applications. 

While differences between cancellous and cortical bone healing may exist, this study concentrates on the healing of cancellous bone within the defect. This animal model is developed to improve future investigations of bone graft substitutes that would interact with cancellous bone. Therefore, it is important to appropriately characterize this region. 

In this pilot study, three different defect diameters of fixed depth were compared in both 18-month-old and 5-year-old sheep. This study was undertaken to investigate the influence of age and defect size on bone healing.

Introduction and framing
Animal model choices in exosome studies for bone regeneration have shifted over recent years to better align with human skeletal biology, disease mechanisms, and clinical delivery contexts, thereby improving construct and external validity. <cite id="d0822b81-0">Systematic assessments of preclinical animal studies show that mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) exosomes promote new bone formation and improved histological, biomechanical, and angiogenic outcomes across diverse bone defect and disease models</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-0">These findings support a trajectory toward clinical translation and emphasize that model selection increasingly reflects the spectrum of clinical indications such as osteonecrosis and osteoporosis</cite>.

From rodent/rabbit defect models to osteoporotic and implant-inclusive paradigms
Early preclinical programs relied heavily on rodent calvarial defects, fracture, distraction osteogenesis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss models to demonstrate osteogenic activity and angiogenesis. <cite id="303db0c5-2">A systematic review cataloged six animal models—calvaria defects, fractures, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss—to mirror clinical conditions spanning trauma, degeneration, congenital deformities, tumor resections, and idiopathic loss</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-1">Across these rodent and rabbit models, exosomes consistently improved osteogenic differentiation and bone formation, with in vivo readouts including microCT and histology</cite>. 

A key evolution has been the inclusion of osteoporosis models that recapitulate patient pathophysiology—osteoclast–osteoblast imbalance, trabecular loss, and delayed healing—providing higher external validity than simple defect filling. <cite id="d4b660d2-0">Bovine milk–derived exosomes reversed multiple osteoporotic phenotypes in mouse models, increasing bone mineral density and bone volume fraction and restoring trabecular microstructure after glucocorticoid-induced or ovariectomy-induced osteoporosis</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-2">The same systematic review documented exosome efficacy across osteoporotic and osteonecrotic contexts and highlighted source and dosing as major variables shaping outcomes</cite>. In parallel, integration with clinically relevant matrices and fixation constructs has grown, reflecting translational delivery routes and composite therapies. <cite id="303db0c5-1">Preclinical work pairing osteoblast-derived exosomes with 3D-printed HA/TCP scaffolds tested osteoconductive and osteogenic augmentation in rabbit calvaria and osteoinductive activity in heterotopic mouse models</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-3">Concurrently, engineered exosome–biomaterial systems have emerged, with authors emphasizing that refining isolation, purification, and storage improves exosome production consistency and that synergy with biomaterials can exceed additive effects for bone regeneration</cite>.

Species and source choices moving toward human-relevant translational validity
Animal selection has evolved from small rodents and rabbits to include larger models and human or well-characterized human-derived sources to better predict pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and tissue response. <cite id="303db0c5-0">Syntheses of current animal studies note that the majority of preclinical samples have been rats, mice, and rabbits, but they explicitly call for further studies in large animal models to establish safety and efficacy prior to clinical trials</cite>. This call reflects the translational rationale: larger species offer skeletal size, architecture, and healing biology closer to humans and more realistic load-bearing and implant interfaces. 

Complementing species shifts, exosome source has become a primary lever for validity and potency. <cite id="303db0c5-2">Source-related variables—tissue anatomical origin and developmental age of donor cells—significantly affect exosome potency for bone regeneration</cite>. <cite id="0f771572-3">For example, young plasma–derived exosomes improved osteoporotic bone regeneration by enhancing BMSC proliferation, migration, and osteogenic differentiation, with miR-217-5p highlighted as a key mediator</cite>. <cite id="0f771572-4">Muscle-derived exosomes have also shown partial facilitation of osteogenesis in osteoporosis models, underscoring that non-classic sources can be therapeutically active</cite>. Importantly, autologous human sources and clinically relevant dosing/delivery paradigms are increasingly represented. <cite id="d4b660d2-0">Oral administration of bovine colostrum-derived exosomes in osteoporotic mouse models improved bone microstructure and preserved trabecular architecture, illustrating feasibility of non-invasive delivery and pointing to gut–bone axis interactions relevant to human disease</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-2">Across models, dosing/concentration and culture preconditioning (e.g., hypoxia or pharmacologic agents) modulate angiogenic and osteogenic potency, reinforcing the need to standardize these variables</cite>.

Methodological maturation: EV characterization, engineering, and reporting standards
Improvements in EV isolation, purification, and characterization have strengthened internal validity by reducing batch-to-batch variability and clarifying cargo and function. <cite id="d0822b81-3">Reviews emphasize that refining EV isolation/purification/storage enhances production consistency; engineering strategies and advanced delivery systems are being combined to exploit exosome–biomaterial synergies</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-0">Methodological reporting has also matured: systematic reviews note unclear-to-low risk in bias and incomplete outcome reporting across primary studies and urge standardization of outcome measurements and reporting to improve comparability</cite>. These methodological advances are matched by delivery realism: pairing EVs with clinically relevant scaffolds and implantable matrices, and testing orthotopic and heterotopic bone sites with longitudinal imaging and histology. <cite id="303db0c5-1">Rabbit calvarial and heterotopic mouse models have been used to test osteoconductive/inductive activity of osteoblast-derived exosomes on ceramic scaffolds, with µCT and histology quantifying neobone formation</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-1">At the same time, authors acknowledge mechanistic gaps and the need for longer-duration animal studies to assess durability and stability of engineered exosome systems</cite>.

Disease-focused and composite-context models: osteoporosis, infection, and implant integration
A second validity gain comes from modeling the comorbidity and composite therapy of human care. <cite id="303db0c5-2">Osteoporotic and osteonecrotic models are now prominent, reflecting clinical scenarios where bone regeneration is impeded by metabolic and vascular pathology</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-0">Beyond simple defects, these models capture osteoclast–osteoblast imbalance and angiogenic coupling, yielding outcomes that include improved bone volume fraction, trabecular architecture, and biomechanics</cite>. Emerging work also explores peri-implant and infection-related contexts relevant to orthopedic and dental regeneration, where exosomes may modulate inflammation, osteogenesis, and integration. <cite id="d0822b81-4">Recent reviews synthesize exosome biology, delivery systems, and preclinical evidence in bone, highlighting translational opportunities and challenges across infection/inflammation and implant contact scenarios</cite>. 

Human–animal bridges and autologous paradigms
The evolution toward translational validity has included bridging from human sources to animal efficacy and, conversely, leveraging animal models to test human-derived exosomes at clinically plausible doses and routes. <cite id="0f771572-3">Young plasma–derived exosomes improved osteoporotic phenotypes in vivo, providing a translational rationale for age-related cargo differences and donor conditioning</cite>. <cite id="d4b660d2-0">Similarly, bovine milk–derived exosomes produced robust skeletal and microbiome rescue in osteoporotic mice with oral delivery, aligning with human-relevant administration and mechanistic complexity (gut–bone axis)</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-2">Across these studies, exosome source and dosing are recognized as central drivers of efficacy, with hypoxia or small-molecule preconditioning enhancing angiogenic osteogenic potential</cite>. These bridges support the emergence of autologous strategies in the clinic, where exosomes are derived from the same patient to minimize immunogenicity and maximize trophic signaling, and they justify the use of human-relevant sources in preclinical testing.

Remaining gaps and trajectory
Although the field has progressed, evidence gaps constrain cross-species generalization and clinical readiness. <cite id="303db0c5-0">Systematic reviews explicitly call for larger animal studies to establish safety and efficacy before human trials</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-1">Methodological limitations include limited study duration, incomplete mechanistic delineation of exosome–cellular pathways, and the need for larger-scale preclinical evaluations to test feasibility and safety</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-0">Incomplete reporting and unclear risk of bias further impede synthesis and comparability, motivating adoption of standardized reporting guidelines and outcome measures</cite>. As these gaps close—via larger species models, human or autologous exosome sources, clinically realistic delivery and implant interfaces, and rigorous EV characterization and reporting—the animal model landscape for exosome-based bone regeneration will continue to evolve toward higher construct and external validity, strengthening the translational pipeline toward clinical deployment. <cite id="d0822b81-0">Collectively, preclinical studies support the translational basis of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-4">Converging biology, engineering, and delivery innovations point to clinically viable exosome therapeutics for skeletal tissue repair</cite>.

Introduction and framing
Animal model choices in exosome studies for bone regeneration have shifted over recent years to better align with human skeletal biology, disease mechanisms, and clinical delivery contexts, thereby improving construct and external validity. <cite id="d0822b81-0">Systematic assessments of preclinical animal studies show that mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) exosomes promote new bone formation and improved histological, biomechanical, and angiogenic outcomes across diverse bone defect and disease models</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-0">These findings support a trajectory toward clinical translation and emphasize that model selection increasingly reflects the spectrum of clinical indications such as osteonecrosis and osteoporosis</cite>.

From rodent/rabbit defect models to osteoporotic and implant-inclusive paradigms
Early preclinical programs relied heavily on rodent calvarial defects, fracture, distraction osteogenesis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss models to demonstrate osteogenic activity and angiogenesis. <cite id="303db0c5-2">A systematic review cataloged six animal models—calvaria defects, fractures, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss—to mirror clinical conditions spanning trauma, degeneration, congenital deformities, tumor resections, and idiopathic loss</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-1">Across these rodent and rabbit models, exosomes consistently improved osteogenic differentiation and bone formation, with in vivo readouts including microCT and histology</cite>. 

A key evolution has been the inclusion of osteoporosis models that recapitulate patient pathophysiology—osteoclast–osteoblast imbalance, trabecular loss, and delayed healing—providing higher external validity than simple defect filling. <cite id="d4b660d2-0">Bovine milk–derived exosomes reversed multiple osteoporotic phenotypes in mouse models, increasing bone mineral density and bone volume fraction and restoring trabecular microstructure after glucocorticoid-induced or ovariectomy-induced osteoporosis</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-2">The same systematic review documented exosome efficacy across osteoporotic and osteonecrotic contexts and highlighted source and dosing as major variables shaping outcomes</cite>. In parallel, integration with clinically relevant matrices and fixation constructs has grown, reflecting translational delivery routes and composite therapies. <cite id="303db0c5-1">Preclinical work pairing osteoblast-derived exosomes with 3D-printed HA/TCP scaffolds tested osteoconductive and osteogenic augmentation in rabbit calvaria and osteoinductive activity in heterotopic mouse models</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-3">Concurrently, engineered exosome–biomaterial systems have emerged, with authors emphasizing that refining isolation, purification, and storage improves exosome production consistency and that synergy with biomaterials can exceed additive effects for bone regeneration</cite>.

Species and source choices moving toward human-relevant translational validity
Animal selection has evolved from small rodents and rabbits to include larger models and human or well-characterized human-derived sources to better predict pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and tissue response. <cite id="303db0c5-0">Syntheses of current animal studies note that the majority of preclinical samples have been rats, mice, and rabbits, but they explicitly call for further studies in large animal models to establish safety and efficacy prior to clinical trials</cite>. This call reflects the translational rationale: larger species offer skeletal size, architecture, and healing biology closer to humans and more realistic load-bearing and implant interfaces. 

Complementing species shifts, exosome source has become a primary lever for validity and potency. <cite id="303db0c5-2">Source-related variables—tissue anatomical origin and developmental age of donor cells—significantly affect exosome potency for bone regeneration</cite>. <cite id="0f771572-3">For example, young plasma–derived exosomes improved osteoporotic bone regeneration by enhancing BMSC proliferation, migration, and osteogenic differentiation, with miR-217-5p highlighted as a key mediator</cite>. <cite id="0f771572-4">Muscle-derived exosomes have also shown partial facilitation of osteogenesis in osteoporosis models, underscoring that non-classic sources can be therapeutically active</cite>. Importantly, autologous human sources and clinically relevant dosing/delivery paradigms are increasingly represented. <cite id="d4b660d2-0">Oral administration of bovine colostrum-derived exosomes in osteoporotic mouse models improved bone microstructure and preserved trabecular architecture, illustrating feasibility of non-invasive delivery and pointing to gut–bone axis interactions relevant to human disease</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-2">Across models, dosing/concentration and culture preconditioning (e.g., hypoxia or pharmacologic agents) modulate angiogenic and osteogenic potency, reinforcing the need to standardize these variables</cite>.

Methodological maturation: EV characterization, engineering, and reporting standards
Improvements in EV isolation, purification, and characterization have strengthened internal validity by reducing batch-to-batch variability and clarifying cargo and function. <cite id="d0822b81-3">Reviews emphasize that refining EV isolation/purification/storage enhances production consistency; engineering strategies and advanced delivery systems are being combined to exploit exosome–biomaterial synergies</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-0">Methodological reporting has also matured: systematic reviews note unclear-to-low risk in bias and incomplete outcome reporting across primary studies and urge standardization of outcome measurements and reporting to improve comparability</cite>. These methodological advances are matched by delivery realism: pairing EVs with clinically relevant scaffolds and implantable matrices, and testing orthotopic and heterotopic bone sites with longitudinal imaging and histology. <cite id="303db0c5-1">Rabbit calvarial and heterotopic mouse models have been used to test osteoconductive/inductive activity of osteoblast-derived exosomes on ceramic scaffolds, with µCT and histology quantifying neobone formation</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-1">At the same time, authors acknowledge mechanistic gaps and the need for longer-duration animal studies to assess durability and stability of engineered exosome systems</cite>.

Disease-focused and composite-context models: osteoporosis, infection, and implant integration
A second validity gain comes from modeling the comorbidity and composite therapy of human care. <cite id="303db0c5-2">Osteoporotic and osteonecrotic models are now prominent, reflecting clinical scenarios where bone regeneration is impeded by metabolic and vascular pathology</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-0">Beyond simple defects, these models capture osteoclast–osteoblast imbalance and angiogenic coupling, yielding outcomes that include improved bone volume fraction, trabecular architecture, and biomechanics</cite>. Emerging work also explores peri-implant and infection-related contexts relevant to orthopedic and dental regeneration, where exosomes may modulate inflammation, osteogenesis, and integration. <cite id="d0822b81-4">Recent reviews synthesize exosome biology, delivery systems, and preclinical evidence in bone, highlighting translational opportunities and challenges across infection/inflammation and implant contact scenarios</cite>. 

Human–animal bridges and autologous paradigms
The evolution toward translational validity has included bridging from human sources to animal efficacy and, conversely, leveraging animal models to test human-derived exosomes at clinically plausible doses and routes. <cite id="0f771572-3">Young plasma–derived exosomes improved osteoporotic phenotypes in vivo, providing a translational rationale for age-related cargo differences and donor conditioning</cite>. <cite id="d4b660d2-0">Similarly, bovine milk–derived exosomes produced robust skeletal and microbiome rescue in osteoporotic mice with oral delivery, aligning with human-relevant administration and mechanistic complexity (gut–bone axis)</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-2">Across these studies, exosome source and dosing are recognized as central drivers of efficacy, with hypoxia or small-molecule preconditioning enhancing angiogenic osteogenic potential</cite>. These bridges support the emergence of autologous strategies in the clinic, where exosomes are derived from the same patient to minimize immunogenicity and maximize trophic signaling, and they justify the use of human-relevant sources in preclinical testing.

Remaining gaps and trajectory
Although the field has progressed, evidence gaps constrain cross-species generalization and clinical readiness. <cite id="303db0c5-0">Systematic reviews explicitly call for larger animal studies to establish safety and efficacy before human trials</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-1">Methodological limitations include limited study duration, incomplete mechanistic delineation of exosome–cellular pathways, and the need for larger-scale preclinical evaluations to test feasibility and safety</cite>. <cite id="303db0c5-0">Incomplete reporting and unclear risk of bias further impede synthesis and comparability, motivating adoption of standardized reporting guidelines and outcome measures</cite>. As these gaps close—via larger species models, human or autologous exosome sources, clinically realistic delivery and implant interfaces, and rigorous EV characterization and reporting—the animal model landscape for exosome-based bone regeneration will continue to evolve toward higher construct and external validity, strengthening the translational pipeline toward clinical deployment. <cite id="d0822b81-0">Collectively, preclinical studies support the translational basis of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration</cite>. <cite id="d0822b81-4">Converging biology, engineering, and delivery innovations point to clinically viable exosome therapeutics for skeletal tissue repair</cite>.

Title: The Role of Bovine Milk-Derived Exosomes in Human Health and Disease
Snippet: Osteoporosis, characterized by loss of bone mass and structural deterioration, is one of the most common metabolic bone diseases, particularly prevalent in the aging population. Its pathogenesis involves an imbalance between two cell types: osteoblasts, which mediate bone formation, and osteoclasts, which are responsible for bone resorption [51]. In recent years, bovine-milk-derived exosomes have been shown to have beneficial effects on bone health. 

The results of the in vitro studies indicated that bovine milk-derived exosomes supported the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts [52], promoted osteoblast proliferation, and accelerated osteoblastogenesis [53]. These promising results were further confirmed by in vivo studies. In a mouse model of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, oral administration of bovine colostrum-derived exosomes prevented bone loss and preserved the microstructure of trabecular bone in the femur [54]. Exosome treatment resulted in a significant increase in both bone mineral density and bone volume percentage compared to the control group, reversing the effects of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis. In addition, a beneficial effect of exosomes on the gut microbiota was observed, which may indicate the existence of a gut-bone axis affecting bone metabolism. In particular, Lactobacillus and Bacteroides, which were both significantly reduced in the osteoporosis model group, were restored to levels similar to those observed in controls in animals treated with exosomes [54]. 

In another study using an ovariectomy-induced mouse model of osteoporosis, bovine milk-derived exosomes also showed protective effects on bone tissue [55]. Exosomes were administered orally to the animals and effectively inhibited osteoclast differentiation, improved bone microstructure, and restored the levels of osteoporosis biomarkers. Microstructural improvements included increased trabecular thickness and bone mineral density in exosome-treated mice compared to untreated animals with osteoporosis.

Title: Stem cell-based bioregenerative therapy of osteoporosis: literature review
Snippet: Aging is an inevitable process of our civilization. Since ancient times, scientists have tried to solve the mystery of aging. The research continues to this day. The most common diseases of old age are disorders of the musculoskeletal system. Among them, osteoporosis continues to occupy the third place in the structure of overall morbidity and mortality. Such statistical data make us think about the search for a possible cause of the disease at the molecular level. The purpose of this study was to analyze the literature data on modern directions of osteoporosis treatment, including stem-cells based bioregenerative medicine. An analytical review of literature data was conducted using the information analysis of Medline (PubMed), Web of Science and Scopus databases, Google Scholar and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) from 2018 to 2022 using the keywords “osteoporosis”, bioregenerative therapy”, “stem cell therapy”. Recent results of preclinical experimental studies have shown the effectiveness of the introduction of new bioregenerative technologies. Preclinical studies on MSC transplantation in the treatment of osteoporosis indicate an increase in osteogenic differentiation, an increase in BMD. Exosomes also may play multiple roles in the treatment of osteoporosis: improving the disbalance between osteoclasts and osteoblasts, structural modification of exosomes and transmitters’ drug function. The promotion of bone regeneration of exosomes has been shown in animal models. Exosomes with active ingredients can treat a variety of skeletal disorders including osteoporosis and osteoporotic fractures. The results of recent research of the bone disorder treatment based on stem cells therapy have shown convincing prospects for new approaches.

Osteoporosis, characterized by loss of bone mass and structural deterioration, is one of the most common metabolic bone diseases, particularly prevalent in the aging population. Its pathogenesis involves an imbalance between two cell types: osteoblasts, which mediate bone formation, and osteoclasts, which are responsible for bone resorption [51]. In recent years, bovine-milk-derived exosomes have been shown to have beneficial effects on bone health. 

The results of the in vitro studies indicated that bovine milk-derived exosomes supported the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts [52], promoted osteoblast proliferation, and accelerated osteoblastogenesis [53]. These promising results were further confirmed by in vivo studies. In a mouse model of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, oral administration of bovine colostrum-derived exosomes prevented bone loss and preserved the microstructure of trabecular bone in the femur [54]. Exosome treatment resulted in a significant increase in both bone mineral density and bone volume percentage compared to the control group, reversing the effects of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis. In addition, a beneficial effect of exosomes on the gut microbiota was observed, which may indicate the existence of a gut-bone axis affecting bone metabolism. In particular, Lactobacillus and Bacteroides, which were both significantly reduced in the osteoporosis model group, were restored to levels similar to those observed in controls in animals treated with exosomes [54]. 

In another study using an ovariectomy-induced mouse model of osteoporosis, bovine milk-derived exosomes also showed protective effects on bone tissue [55]. Exosomes were administered orally to the animals and effectively inhibited osteoclast differentiation, improved bone microstructure, and restored the levels of osteoporosis biomarkers. Microstructural improvements included increased trabecular thickness and bone mineral density in exosome-treated mice compared to untreated animals with osteoporosis.

Title: Mesenchymal stem cell exosomes in bone regenerative strategies—a systematic review of preclinical studies
Snippet: The ability of bone for regeneration has long been recognized. However, once beyond a critical size, spontaneous regeneration of bone is limited. Several studies have focused on enhancing bone regeneration by applying mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (MSCs) in the treatment strategies. Despite the therapeutic efficacy of MSCs in bone regeneration, cell-based therapies are impeded by several challenges in maintaining the optimal cell potency and viability during expansion, storage, and final delivery to patients. Recently, there has been a paradigm shift in therapeutic mechanism of MSCs in tissue repair from one based on cellular differentiation and replacement to one based on secretion and paracrine signaling. Among the broad spectrum of trophic factors, extracellular vesicles particularly the exosomes have been reported to be therapeutically efficacious in several injury/disease indications, including bone defects and diseases. The current systematic review aims to summarize the results of the existing animal studies which were conducted to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis guidelines, the PubMed and The Cochrane Library database were searched for relevant controlled preclinical animal studies. A total of 23 studies were identified, with the total sample size being 690 rats or mice and 38 rabbits. Generally, MSC exosomes were found to be efficacious for bone regeneration in animal models of bone defects and diseases such as osteonecrosis and osteoporosis. In these studies, MSC exosomes promoted new bone formation with supporting vasculature and displayed improved morphological, biomechanical, and histological outcomes, coupled with positive effects on cell survival, proliferation, and migration, osteogenesis, and angiogenesis. Unclear-to-low risk in bias and incomplete reporting in the primary studies highlighted the need for standardization in outcome measurements and reporting. Snippet: The principal finding of this systematic review is that MSC exosomes are therapeutically efficacious in bone regeneration. This therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes in bone regeneration is demonstrated by the formation of new bone with supporting vasculature and improved morphological, biomechanical, and histological outcomes, in the studies reviewed . 

Six different animal models of bone defects and diseases were used in these studies to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. These included animal models of calvaria defects, fractures, distraction osteogenesis, osteoporosis, osteonecrosis, and irradiation-induced bone loss that reflect the various clinical conditions that could result in bone defects or bone loss, including trauma, degeneration, congenital deformities, tumor resections and idiopathic conditions . Through this systematic review, it was noted that irrespective of the models used, MSC exosomes were found to exhibit prolific therapeutic efficacy in bone regeneration for the various bone defects and diseases, and no adverse effects associated with the use of MSC exosomes were reported from those studies . 

Despite the therapeutic efficacy of MSC exosomes, several factors/ variables have been identified to likely influence the outcome of intervention with the use of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration. These factors included primarily the source and dosage/concentration of MSC exosomes. With regards to the source of exosomes, the anatomical origin and developmental age of the tissues for isolation of MSCs reportedly influenced the potency of MSC exosomes for bone regeneration [49,57]. The culture condition of MSCs also affects the potency of isolated exosomes. By means of preconditioning with small molecules such as dimethyloxaloylglycine [50] or hypoxia stimulation [53], these studies demonstrated that such culture manipulation of MSCs could enhance the potency of MSC exosomes in angiogenesis and henceforth promote bone regeneration.
